claim: In 1984, Davor Solter (working with James McGrath) and independently Azim Surani (working with Sheila Barton and Michael Norris) published results of experiments on newly fertilized mouse eggs where they generated embryos containing either two sets of maternal chromosomes or two sets of paternal chromosomes.
source: In 1984, Davor Solter (working with James McGrath at the Wistar Institute in Philadelphia) and, independently, Azim Surani (working with Sheila Barton and Michael Norris at the AFRC Institute of Animal Physiology in Cambridge) published the results of experiments on newly fertilized mouse eggs (McGrath and Solter, 1984; Surani et al., 1984; Barton et al., 1984). They had generated embryos that contained either two sets of chromosomes inherited from the mother, or two sets of chromosomes inherited from the father.
evidence: Supported by citations to McGrath and Solter, 1984; Surani et al., 1984; Barton et al., 1984

claim: Embryos with either two maternal or two paternal chromosome sets failed to develop to term when transferred into pseudo-pregnant recipient females.
source: However, when transferred into pseudo-pregnant recipient females, the embryos failed to develop to term.
evidence: Supported by citations to the 1984 publications in the preceding sentence

claim: The set of chromosomes inherited from the mother are not functionally equivalent to the set inherited from the father despite being genetically equivalent.
source: These remarkable results sent a clear message: despite being genetically equivalent, the set of chromosomes inherited from the mother were not functionally equivalent to the set inherited from the father.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results described in the cited 1984 publications

claim: Normal development requires one set of chromosomes from each parent due to genomic imprinting.
source: The defective development of the bi-maternal and the bi-paternal embryos indicated that, for normal development to occur, one set of chromosomes from each parent was required. This is due to a process called 'genomic imprinting' which acts in the gametes to 'mark' genes on the maternal and paternal chromosomes in order to ensure parent-of-origin specific expression after fertilization.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations of defective development in uniparental embryos

claim: Genomic imprinting acts in the gametes to mark genes on maternal and paternal chromosomes to ensure parent-of-origin specific expression after fertilization.
source: This is due to a process called 'genomic imprinting' which acts in the gametes to 'mark' genes on the maternal and paternal chromosomes in order to ensure parent-of-origin specific expression after fertilization.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about genomic imprinting mechanism

claim: Cells express only one copy of an imprinted gene, either the copy inherited from the father or the copy inherited from the mother.
source: However, cells express only one copy of an imprinted gene – either the copy inherited from the father or the copy inherited from the mother.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about imprinted gene expression

claim: The imprinting marks are epigenetic modifications, in particular DNA methylation.
source: It later emerged that the imprinting marks were epigenetic modifications (in particular, DNA methylation).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge that emerged after the initial discovery

claim: Imprinted genes are not evenly distributed across the whole genome but located in particular genomic regions.
source: Around the same time, genetic studies by Bruce Cattanach and Michael Kirk showed that imprinted genes were not evenly distributed across the whole genome but located in particular genomic regions (Cattanach and Kirk, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cattanach and Kirk, 1985

claim: The first three imprinted genes identified were Igf2r, Igf2 and H19, which were not identified until 1991.
source: This finding was confirmed by the subsequent identification and mapping of imprinted genes, although the first three imprinted genes, Igf2r, Igf2 and H19, were not identified until 1991 (Barlow et al., 1991; DeChiara et al., 1991; Ferguson-Smith et al., 1991; Bartolomei et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to four 1991 publications

claim: Imprinted genes are essential for prenatal development of normal embryonic and extraembryonic components.
source: Over the years, studies in mice and humans have shown that imprinted genes are essential not only for the prenatal development of normal embryonic and extraembryonic components, as demonstrated in the early experiments of Surani and Solter, but also for postnatal processes that include the regulation of the brain and behavior, metabolism, and physiological adaptations (Cleaton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cleaton et al., 2014 and reference to early experiments

claim: Imprinted genes are essential for postnatal processes including regulation of the brain and behavior, metabolism, and physiological adaptations.
source: Over the years, studies in mice and humans have shown that imprinted genes are essential not only for the prenatal development of normal embryonic and extraembryonic components, as demonstrated in the early experiments of Surani and Solter, but also for postnatal processes that include the regulation of the brain and behavior, metabolism, and physiological adaptations (Cleaton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cleaton et al., 2014

claim: Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome is a fetal overgrowth disorder associated with an increased incidence of childhood tumors.
source: Moreover, a number of human syndromes exhibiting parent-of-origin effects in their patterns of inheritance were known, including the fetal overgrowth disorder Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome (which is also associated with an increased incidence of childhood tumors), and two neurological disorders (Prader-Willi Syndrome and Angelman Syndrome).
evidence: Established medical knowledge about the syndrome

claim: Prader-Willi Syndrome and Angelman Syndrome are neurological disorders exhibiting parent-of-origin effects.
source: Moreover, a number of human syndromes exhibiting parent-of-origin effects in their patterns of inheritance were known, including the fetal overgrowth disorder Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome (which is also associated with an increased incidence of childhood tumors), and two neurological disorders (Prader-Willi Syndrome and Angelman Syndrome).
evidence: Established medical knowledge about these syndromes

claim: Imprinting disorders are caused by inheritance of two imprinted domains from one parent and none from the other, deletions at imprinted regions, or failure to establish or maintain proper imprints.
source: These and other syndromes were found to be caused by the inheritance of two imprinted domains from the mother and none from the father, or vice versa; by deletions at imprinted regions; or by a failure either to establish a proper imprint during gamete production or to maintain it after fertilization.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about mechanisms of imprinting disorders

claim: Imprinted genes are implicated in pathways that control the aetiology of common diseases such as those involved in growth, metabolism, cancer and neurological disorders.
source: Such studies have, of course, been important for elucidating these imprinted disorders, but perhaps more importantly, they have implicated imprinted genes more generally in pathways that control the aetiology of much more common diseases, such as those involved in growth, metabolism, cancer and neurological disorders.
evidence: Inference from studies on imprinted disorders

claim: Genomic imprinting involves transmission of epigenetic information in the form of DNA methylation marks from gametes to offspring, resulting in around 100-200 genes being expressed from only one chromosome.
source: We now know that genomic imprinting involves the transmission of epigenetic information, in the form of DNA methylation marks, from gametes to offspring, with the result that a set of around 100–200 genes (both protein coding genes and non-coding RNA genes) are expressed from only one of the two chromosomes in cells.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about genomic imprinting

claim: The essential role for DNA methylation in imprinting was shown through the inheritance of mutations in DNA methyltransferases.
source: The essential role for DNA methylation in imprinting was shown through the inheritance of mutations in DNA methyltransferases (Bourc'his et al., 2001; Li et al., 1993; Kaneda et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to three publications on DNA methyltransferase mutations

claim: DNA methylation marks are acted upon by a hierarchy of transcriptional and chromatin states, including differential histone modifications on the two parental chromosomes, resulting in monoallelic expression of imprinted genes.
source: These DNA methylation marks provide an imprint that is acted upon by a hierarchy of transcriptional and chromatin states, including differential histone modifications on the two parental chromosomes (Fournier et al., 2002), that result in the monoallelic expression of imprinted genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fournier et al., 2002

claim: Imprinted genes are often clustered around a single imprinting control region (ICR) that influences the monoallelic expression of the whole cluster.
source: It also became clear that imprinted genes are often clustered around a single imprinting control region (ICR) that influences the monoallelic expression of the whole cluster.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about ICR organization

claim: ICRs are regulatory sequences that control the expression of genes coding for proteins or long-non-coding RNAs that control cluster activity in cis.
source: Indeed, ICRs are regulatory sequences that control the expression of genes that code for proteins, or for long-non-coding RNAs that control the activity of the cluster in cis.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about ICR function

claim: The transcription factor CTCF has an important role at some imprinted clusters to modulate regulation of imprinted gene expression in a parental-origin-specific manner.
source: A transcription factor called CTCF also has an important role at some (but not all) of these clusters, to modulate the regulation of imprinted gene expression in a parental-origin-specific manner.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CTCF function

claim: Analysis of differential DNA methylation at imprinted domains has provided a paradigm to assess links between epigenetic states and cis-acting control of gene expression in mammals.
source: Hence, over the years, the analysis of differential DNA methylation at imprinted domains has provided a paradigm in which to assess the links between particular epigenetic states and the long- and short-range cis-acting control of gene expression in mammals.
evidence: Summary of scientific progress in the field

claim: Studies on imprinted domains have uncovered regulatory relationships between DNA methylation, histone modifications, long-non-coding RNAs and associated proteins, and helped define enzymatic processes that write, read and erase epigenetic states.
source: These studies have uncovered regulatory relationships between DNA methylation, histone modifications, long-non-coding RNAs and associated proteins (such as CTCF), and has helped to define many of the enzymatic processes that write, read and erase epigenetic states (Barlow and Bartolomei, 2014; Ferguson-Smith, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to two review articles

claim: Genome-wide profiling of gametic methylation in mice and humans has revealed that thousands of sequences acquire asymmetric DNA methylation states in the oocyte and spermatozoon.
source: In particular, genome-wide profiling of gametic methylation in mice and humans has highlighted that thousands of sequences acquire asymmetric DNA methylation states in the oocyte and spermatozoon, reflecting the contrasting biology of DNA methylation in the two germlines (Smallwood et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smallwood et al., 2011 and Kobayashi et al., 2012

claim: In males, sperm methylation preferentially targets intergenic sequences and transposon repeats.
source: In males, sperm methylation preferentially targets intergenic sequences and transposon repeats.
evidence: Inference from genome-wide profiling studies cited in the preceding sentence

claim: In females, oocyte methylation coincides with the body of actively transcribed genes, including intragenic CpG islands.
source: In females, oocyte methylation coincides with the body of actively transcribed genes, including intragenic CpG islands (Veselovska et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Veselovska et al., 2015

claim: Maternal ICRs all coincide with CpG island promoters located downstream of transcription start sites that are active during oocyte growth.
source: The distribution and genomic properties of ICRs do not differ from these genome-wide trends: maternal ICRs all coincide with CpG island promoters located downstream of transcription start sites that are active during oocyte growth, while paternal ICRs have an intergenic location.
evidence: Inference from genome-wide methylation profiling data

claim: Paternal ICRs have an intergenic location.
source: The distribution and genomic properties of ICRs do not differ from these genome-wide trends: maternal ICRs all coincide with CpG island promoters located downstream of transcription start sites that are active during oocyte growth, while paternal ICRs have an intergenic location.
evidence: Inference from genome-wide methylation profiling data

claim: ICRs are not established as special regulators in the germline but are selected post-fertilization by being actively protected from genome-wide loss of methylation before embryo implantation.
source: ICRs are not established as special regulators in the germline: rather they are selected, post-fertilization, by being actively protected from the genome-wide loss of methylation that occurs before embryo implantation.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about ICR establishment and maintenance

claim: ICRs are endowed with several TGCCGC motifs that, when methylated, are recognized by zinc finger protein ZFP57.
source: ICRs are endowed with several TGCCGC motifs and, when methylated, these motifs are recognized by a zinc finger protein called ZFP57 which, in turn, recruits the KAP1-centered heterochromatic complex (Quenneville et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quenneville et al., 2011

claim: ZFP57 recruits the KAP1-centered heterochromatic complex upon recognizing methylated TGCCGC motifs.
source: ICRs are endowed with several TGCCGC motifs and, when methylated, these motifs are recognized by a zinc finger protein called ZFP57 which, in turn, recruits the KAP1-centered heterochromatic complex (Quenneville et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quenneville et al., 2011

claim: ZFP57-KAP1 complex allows for concentration of DNA methyltransferases around ICRs and propagation of germline-methylation status in the early embryo during global reprogramming.
source: This allows for the concentration of DNA methyltransferases around the ICRs and the propagation of their germline-methylation status in the early embryo, while the rest of the genome is undergoing global reprogramming.
evidence: Inference from the mechanism described with ZFP57 and KAP1

claim: Complete depletion of ZFP57 causes multiple ICRs to fail to maintain their parental methylation imprint after fertilization, leading to misregulation of imprinted expression and embryonic lethality.
source: Upon complete depletion of ZFP57, multiple ICRs fail to maintain their parental methylation imprint after fertilization, leading to misregulation of imprinted expression and embryonic lethality (Li et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2008

claim: All cases of epigenetic intergenerational inheritance may follow the molecular principle that genomic sequences acquiring methylation during gametogenesis must be recognized by methyl-sensitive, sequence-specific DNA binding factors to persist in the next generation.
source: More generally, all cases of epigenetic intergenerational inheritance – both normal and pathological – may follow the same molecular principle: to persist in the next generation, genomic sequences that have acquired methylation during gametogenesis have to be recognized by methyl-sensitive, sequence-specific DNA binding factors (such as ZFP57) to locally attract the DNA methylation enzymes.
evidence: Speculative generalization from ZFP57 mechanism

claim: CpG-rich sequences have a higher probability of containing several TGCCGC motifs and therefore a higher probability of being protected by ZFP57.
source: Incidentally, CpG-rich sequences, such as CpG islands, have a higher probability of containing several TGCCGC motifs and, therefore, a higher probability of being protected by ZFP57.
evidence: Logical inference from sequence composition

claim: The greater number of maternal ICRs compared to paternal ICRs may be explained by maternal ICRs being CpG-rich promoters with higher probability of ZFP57 protection, while paternal ICRs are intergenic sequences under lower evolutionary pressure to maintain CpG motifs.
source: This may explain the greater number of maternal ICRs (which are CpG-rich promoters) compared to paternal ICRs, which are derived from intergenic sequences and are, therefore, under lower evolutionary pressure to maintain CpG motifs.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on sequence properties

claim: The current census is around 22 maternal ICRs versus three paternal ICRs, for a total of 25 ICRs.
source: The current census is around 22 maternal ICRs versus three paternal ICRs, hence a total of 25 ICRs.
evidence: Data from current genomic surveys

claim: Paternal ICRs have less influence on development than maternal ICRs.
source: Paternal ICRs are not only at a numerical disadvantage, they also have less influence on development than maternal ICRs (Schulz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schulz et al., 2010

claim: Viable bi-maternal mice were produced by aggregating a normal maternally-imprinted genome with a second non-imprinted maternal genome in which the imprinting effects of two of the three paternal ICRs were restored through genetic deletion.
source: Nonetheless, it is noteworthy that among the diverse efforts that followed the original work of Solter and Surani to modify parental imprinting and overcome the barriers to mono-parental reproduction, viable bi-maternal mice were produced (Kawahara et al., 2007). This was done by aggregating a normal maternally-imprinted genome with a second non-imprinted maternal genome in which the imprinting effects of two of the three paternal ICRs were restored through the use of genetic deletion.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kawahara et al., 2007

claim: All canonical ICRs with parent-specific DNA methylation patterns maintained in a life-long and tissue-wide manner have probably been uncovered.
source: Many genome-wide screens have been developed to identify new imprinted loci but the general conclusion is that all the canonical ICRs – that is, those with parent-specific DNA methylation patterns that are maintained in a life-long and tissue-wide manner – have probably been uncovered (Xie et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2012

claim: Less robust ICRs have been detected with parent-specific DNA methylation patterns confined to early embryonic development or persisting in some adult tissues only.
source: Less robust ICRs have been detected, whereby parent-specific DNA methylation patterns are confined to early embryonic development or persist in some adult tissues only (Proudhon et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Proudhon et al., 2012

claim: Stage- and tissue-specific ICRs translate into variations in the allelic dosage of the imprinted genes they regulate.
source: These stage- and tissue-specific ICRs translate into variations in the allelic dosage of the imprinted genes they regulate (Greenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greenberg et al., 2017

claim: Biallelic expression of imprinted genes can occur without modifying the methylation imprint itself, as exemplified by the paternally expressed Dlk1 gene adopting biallelic expression in neural stem cells with important implications for neurogenesis.
source: Biallelic expression of imprinted genes can also occur without modifying the methylation imprint itself: for example, the paternally expressed Dlk1 gene adopts biallelic expression in neural stem cells with important implications for neurogenesis (Ferrón et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferrón et al., 2011

claim: Genomic imprinting is more flexible across the lifetime of an individual than originally thought.
source: These studies have highlighted that genomic imprinting is more flexible across the lifetime of an individual than originally thought.
evidence: Inference from studies on stage- and tissue-specific imprinting variations

claim: Imprinting can be polymorphic between mammalian species, with some ICRs found in rodents but not in humans, and vice versa.
source: But imprinting can also be polymorphic between mammalian species: some ICRs are found in rodents but not in humans, and vice versa (see, for example, https://atlas.genetics.kcl.ac.uk/atlas.php and www.geneimprint.com/site/genes-by-species).
evidence: Supported by reference to online databases

claim: Transposons have acted as major drivers for the emergence of species-specific ICRs.
source: As for many genetic innovations, transposons have acted as major drivers for the emergence of these species-specific ICRs.
evidence: Established knowledge about transposon role in genomic evolution

claim: During spermatogenesis, retrotransposon methylation is guided by piRNAs to ensure germline genome protection.
source: During spermatogenesis, retrotransposon methylation is guided by specific small RNAs called piRNAs (short for PIWI-interacting RNAs) to ensure that the germline genome is protected.
evidence: Established knowledge about piRNA function in spermatogenesis

claim: A retrotransposon that landed into the Rasgrf1 locus in rodents has created a new paternally methylated ICR in these species.
source: Through this mechanism, a retrotransposon that landed into the Rasgrf1 locus in rodents has created a new paternally methylated ICR in these species (Watanabe et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Watanabe et al., 2011

claim: Long terminal repeat (LTR) sequences of specific retrotransposons are particularly active during oogenesis and can define new transcription start sites in oocytes and promote transcription-coupled DNA methylation of downstream CpG islands.
source: Similarly, long terminal repeat (LTR) sequences of specific retrotransposons are particularly active during oogenesis. Through their promoter activity, they can define new transcription start sites in oocytes and promote transcription-coupled DNA methylation of downstream CpG islands (Brind'Amour et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brind'Amour et al., 2018

claim: Rodent- and human-specific insertions containing binding sites for post-fertilization methylation maintenance can diversify the germline methylome and generate new species-specific ICRs.
source: Rodent- and human-specific insertions that contain binding sites for post-fertilization methylation maintenance (by factors such as ZFP57) can, therefore, diversify the germline 'methylome' and generate new species-specific ICRs.
evidence: Inference from transposon insertion mechanisms

claim: Because LTR transposons are still active in rodent genomes, some ICRs are found in some mouse strains but not in others.
source: Furthermore, because LTR transposons are still active in rodent genomes, some ICRs are found in some mouse strains but not in others (Brind'Amour et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brind'Amour et al., 2018

claim: Whether strain-specific ICRs could be phenotypically influential is unknown.
source: Whether these could be phenotypically influential is unknown.
evidence: Explicit statement of lack of knowledge

claim: Genomic imprinting that does not involve DNA methylation has been discovered, involving trimethylation of lysine 27 in histone H3 (H3K27me3).
source: Finally, one of the most intriguing findings of recent years was the discovery of genomic imprinting that does not involve DNA methylation. The trimethylation of lysine 27 in histone H3 (H3K27me3) is an epigenetic mark that is asymmetrically transmitted by parental gametes and remains after fertilization to influence the allelic expression of several genes in the early embryo (Inoue et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inoue et al., 2017

claim: H3K27me3 is an epigenetic mark that is asymmetrically transmitted by parental gametes and remains after fertilization to influence allelic expression of several genes in the early embryo.
source: The trimethylation of lysine 27 in histone H3 (H3K27me3) is an epigenetic mark that is asymmetrically transmitted by parental gametes and remains after fertilization to influence the allelic expression of several genes in the early embryo (Inoue et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inoue et al., 2017

claim: Non-canonical genomic imprinting via H3K27me3 is exclusively transmitted by the oocyte and is only maintained until the blastocyst stage.
source: However, this 'non-canonical' form of genomic imprinting is exclusively transmitted by the oocyte and is only maintained until the blastocyst stage.
evidence: Inference from the study cited in the preceding sentence (Inoue et al., 2017)

claim: By the time of implantation (less than a week after fertilization), the parent-specific differences in H3K27me3 have disappeared.
source: By the time of implantation – less than a week after fertilization – the parent-specific differences have disappeared.
evidence: Inference from the study on H3K27me3 imprinting

claim: Genomic imprinting was discovered at a time when modifications to DNA and chromatin that regulate genome function were only beginning to be appreciated.
source: Genomic imprinting was discovered at a time when the modifications to DNA and chromatin that act 'on top of' genetics and regulate genome function were only beginning to be appreciated.
evidence: Historical context about the state of epigenetics field in the 1980s

claim: The contribution of genomic imprinting to understanding epigenetic mechanisms has been major.
source: The contribution of this essential mammalian developmental process to our understanding of epigenetic mechanisms has been major.
evidence: Summary assessment of the field's impact

claim: Through analysis of active and repressed alleles of imprinted genes within a given cell type during development, robust relationships between regional epigenetic control and transcriptional behavior have been established.
source: Through the analysis of active and repressed alleles of imprinted genes within a given cell type during development, robust relationships between regional epigenetic control and transcriptional behavior have been established.
evidence: Summary of scientific progress in understanding epigenetic regulation

claim: The evolutionary processes that have led to the emergence of genomic imprinting in mammals are not yet understood.
source: Though we still do not understand the evolutionary processes that have led to the emergence of genomic imprinting in mammals, its interrogation over the years has revealed a wealth of epigenetic insight that continues to have an enduring influence on genome biology.
evidence: Explicit statement of lack of understanding

claim: Interrogation of genomic imprinting over the years has revealed a wealth of epigenetic insight that continues to have an enduring influence on genome biology.
source: Though we still do not understand the evolutionary processes that have led to the emergence of genomic imprinting in mammals, its interrogation over the years has revealed a wealth of epigenetic insight that continues to have an enduring influence on genome biology.
evidence: Summary assessment of the field's impact on genome biology

claim: Solter and Surani received a 2018 Canada Gairdner International Award for the discovery of mammalian genomic imprinting that causes parent-of-origin specific gene expression and its consequences for development and disease.
source: This article is being published to celebrate Solter and Surani receiving a 2018 Canada Gairdner International Award "for the discovery of mammalian genomic imprinting that causes parent-of-origin specific gene expression and its consequences for development and disease".
evidence: Factual statement about award
